findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in the convergence ranking (six evidence streams) with upregulation in UC mucosa [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.838], and an Open Targets UC association score of [gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5345]. It has clinical small-molecule antagonists in other indications (reparixin Phase 3; navarixin, ladarixin, danirixin, elubrixin, SX-682 Phase 2), none recorded for UC, so it is an expression- and genetics-led candidate that could be repurposed. Neutrophil degranulation and chemokine receptor signalling are its Reactome pathways.

CXCR2 has no cis-pQTL and no gut eQTL instrument, so Mendelian randomisation is not tested; this is absence of data, not evidence against. Mouse colitis literature exists (many papers, including a selective CXCR2 antagonist ameliorating acute colitis) but MGI records no single-gene colitis phenotype. The gene is not strongly constrained against loss of function and no safety events are recorded.

Genetically higher plasma PD-L1 lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]), colocalises with the IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen (OR [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; finngen_odds_ratio_per_sd=0.734]). Because beta is below zero, PD-L1 inhibitors (approved checkpoint antibodies such as atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab) would act against the protective direction, a mechanistic warning for UC despite CD274 being upregulated in the mucosa.

MR sensitivity for CD274 plasma protein shows Steiger direction correct and a non-significant Egger intercept, but heterogeneity is present (Cochran p [gene=CD274; type=mr_sensitivity; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; layer=plasma_protein; heterogeneity_p=0.0259]) with only three instruments. No known safety events are recorded, and no gut eQTL instrument was available, so blood and gut cannot be compared.

IL12B, a known UC drug target and the top Open Targets UC association, has the strongest plasma MR signal: genetically higher IL12B protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]), colocalising with the IBD GWAS and replicating in FinnGen and in a further independent UC GWAS. This supports IL12B (p40) inhibition as a genetically validated positive control for the method.

CXCL5 is strongly upregulated in UC biopsies and has no approved drug, yet genetically higher plasma CXCL5 lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]), replicating in FinnGen but not colocalising with an IBD GWAS signal (uses a tag variant, two instruments). The direction argues against blocking CXCL5, so the mucosal increase may be a response rather than a driver.

CXCL8 is among the most replicated upregulated genes (eight cohorts same direction) but has zero Open Targets genetic association and the plasma MR is null (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]) and does not replicate in FinnGen. It fits a biomarker of neutrophil-driven inflammation rather than a genetically supported target; anti-IL-8 antibodies (ABX-IL8, adakitug) only reached Phase 2.

Mucosal SLC26A3 falls in UC biopsies, yet genetically predicted gut cell-type expression (IBDverse, OLFM4+ crypt enterocyte progenitors) is positively associated with UC risk (OR per SD [gene=SLC26A3; type=mendelian_randomization_gut; source=DATASET:MR_GUT_EQTL_UC; layer=gut_cell; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.607]), the opposite of what the fall would predict; the estimate colocalises with the IBD GWAS and replicates in FinnGen and a further independent UC GWAS. The mucosal loss is therefore probably a consequence of inflammation while risk alleles act in the other direction; only one instrument and one cell type were tested, plasma and colon-tissue MR are not tested, and no drug exists.

IDO1 is strongly and consistently upregulated (eight cohorts same direction) with no Open Targets genetic association; it is druggable (epacadostat recorded at approval stage in another indication, linrodostat Phase 3) and sits in tryptophan catabolism. Mouse colitis literature is mixed in direction (epithelial IDO1 and IL-10 repression papers), and MGI has no curated colitis phenotype, so direction of benefit is unresolved.

JAK2 is a known UC target class with a high Open Targets association (second among top UC targets) and clinical drugs (fedratinib approved in another indication), but its mucosal expression change is modest compared with inflammatory genes, so it is genetically supported rather than expression-led.

CXCR1 ranks just below CXCR2 in the convergence ranking, is upregulated in UC and shares the same antagonists as CXCR2 (reparixin, ladarixin, navarixin, SX-682), with intermediate Open Targets genetic association; like CXCR2, it has no MR instrument, so the CXCR1 and CXCR2 neutrophil axis rests on expression, association and literature rather than MR.

CHI3L1, AQP9 and S100A8 are strongly upregulated and replicated across cohorts, without Open Targets genetic association or a drug, so they are expression-led biomarker candidates (neutrophil/myeloid activity) rather than genetically supported targets.

caveats: Plasma MR needs a cis-pQTL; CXCR2, CXCR1, IDO1 and most top-ranked genes were not tested, which is not evidence against them.
Only a subset of candidates had MR, mouse and safety queries; the remaining top-40 genes were taken from the convergence ranking only.
MGI had no curated colitis phenotype for CXCR2, CD274, IDO1 or CXCL5; the literature check shows testing, not result.
Drug stages are as returned by Open Targets in any indication, none of the CXCR1, CXCR2, PD-L1 or IDO1 drugs is recorded for UC here.
The SLC26A3 estimate comes from one instrument in one cell type; the CD274 estimate shows heterogeneity across three instruments.
